1022a14: "That in virtue of which" is said in several ways: in one way, the form
1022a15: and the substance of each thing — for example, that in virtue of which a man is good
1022a16: is the good itself; in another way, that in which a thing first comes to be by nature — for example,
1022a19: the primary subject for each thing. In general, "that in virtue of which" will have as many senses as
1022a20: the cause has; for "in virtue of what did he come" or "for the sake of what did he come"
1022a21: is said, and "in virtue of what was he deceived" or "has he reasoned correctly"
1022a24: for all these signify a place and a position. Hence also
1022a25: "per se" must be said in several ways. One sense of
1022a26: per se is the essence of each thing — for instance, Callias per se is
1022a29: animal is present in the account; for animal is something that Callias is. Further,
1022a30: if something has been received in the thing itself primarily or in something of its own — for instance, the surface
1022a31: is white per se, and the man lives per se;
1022a34: animal, the biped, yet nonetheless man per se is man
1022a35: himself. Further, whatever belongs to a thing alone and insofar as it alone, being separated in itself,
